group_assessment.weighting: A minireview by the National Cheng Kung University group that produced much of the WWOX stress, Zfra and mitochondrial-translocation literature; it summarises, with no new measurement. The group studies the gene in cancer and acquired-stress systems, not biallelic-LoF disease. Its mitochondrial statements are weighted as pointers to the primaries behind them.

entries.proposition: Whole-body Wwox knock-out mice die by four weeks, so the review itself says organ-specific ablation is needed; nothing in the review concerns biallelic-LoF disease.
entries.snippet: However, all whole-body Wwox gene knockout mice died by four weeks of age.
entries.anchor: WWOX functions as a tumor suppressor

entries.proposition: Mitochondrial localisation claim 1: constant-light retinal degeneration with nuclear and mitochondrial accumulation of Tyr33-phosphorylated Wwox in rodent photoreceptors (ref 37).
entries.snippet: Constant light-induced retinal degeneration is associated with nuclear and mitochondrial accumulation of Tyr33-phosphorylated Wwox protein in rodent photoreceptors
entries.anchor: WWOX regulates cell apoptosis in stress responses

entries.proposition: Consolidating sentence: WWOX is said to be activated by Tyr33 phosphorylation and to translocate to membrane, mitochondria and nucleus under stress; every cited instance is an acquired stress or cancer-cell context.
entries.snippet: WWOX is activated via phosphorylation at Tyr33 and translocates to the cell membrane, mitochondria, and nucleus under stress conditions
entries.anchor: WWOX regulates cell apoptosis in stress responses

entries.proposition: Respiration claim: WWOX deficiency decreases mitochondrial respiration in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (ref 54), with the mechanism stated as unexplained.
entries.snippet: WWOX deficiency decreases mitochondrial respiration in mouse embryonic fibroblasts.
entries.anchor: WWOX has been linked to the regulation of many TCF (glucose metabolism paragraph)

entries.proposition: The review states the mechanism by which WWOX regulates oxidative phosphorylation is not known.
entries.snippet: The mechanism by which WWOX regulates oxidative phosphorylation in the mitochondria remains to be further investigated.
entries.anchor: WWOX has been linked to the regulation of many TCF (glucose metabolism paragraph)

entries.proposition: HIF-1alpha binding by WWOX and suppression of GLUT1 (ref 54), the glucose-metabolism content of the review.
entries.snippet: WWOX physically interacts with hypoxia-inducible transcription factor 1α (HIF-1α) and suppresses HIF-1α-mediated transcriptional activation of downstream targets
entries.anchor: WWOX has been linked to the regulation of many TCF (glucose metabolism paragraph)

entries.proposition: Zfra: ZFRA and WWOX translocate to mitochondria after TNF or UV and Zfra blocks WWOX-induced cytochrome c release (refs 55, 57); cancer-cell culture contexts.
entries.snippet: Zfra also blocks WWOX-induced cytochrome c release from the mitochondria.
entries.anchor: WWOX participates in multiple signaling pathways

entries.proposition: The catalytic function of the SDR domain is described as uncharacterised.
entries.snippet: Whether WWOX exerts its enzymatic function via binding to its interacting proteins, such as Tau, GSK-3β, and DVL2, for regulating steroid metabolism and redox balance is unclear and remains to be clearly characterized.

entries.proposition: Closing statement on metabolism: recent studies suggest WWOX is a metabolic regulator, flagged as a future goal.
entries.snippet: Recent studies have suggested that WWOX acts as a regulator in metabolic processes.

entries.proposition: The reference list carries one entry twice (the 2001 WWOX tumour-types paper appears as references 5 and 30).
entries.snippet: WWOX: a candidate tumor suppressor gene involved in multiple tumor types.

entries.proposition: Figure 2 is a signalling schematic: stress or TNF acting through Src, Tyr33-phosphorylated WWOX with p53 or JNK1 and Zfra, an arrow from WWOX to a mitochondrion with release dots, and WWOX inhibiting GLI1, DVL2, GSK-3beta, Tau and HIF-1alpha; it plots no data.
entries.snippet: [figure attestation - pixels cannot be quote-matched] Figure 2: scheme with Hyal-2 and TGF-beta at left, Shh-Ptc1-Smo and GLI1, Wnt and DVL2, and at right Stress via Src and TNF to P-WWOX with p53, JNK1 and Zfra, and an arrow to a mitochondrion icon with release dots; central WWOX box with inhibitory lines to GSK-3b, Tau, HIF-1a and an arrow Ack1 to polyubiquitination and degradation; nucleus below with P-WWOX and p53.

entries.proposition: Figure 3 is a speculative schematic of anticancer-drug-induced WWOX upregulation, mTOR, autophagy and mitochondrial caspase activation; most arrows carry question marks and it plots no data.
entries.snippet: [figure attestation - pixels cannot be quote-matched] Figure 3: left chemoresistant cells with autophagosome and survival; right sensitive cells with WWOX, mTOR and p70S6K, LC3, Beclin-1 and ATG5 inhibition, mitochondria with caspase-9 and caspase-3 to apoptosis; several arrows marked with question marks.

entries.proposition: Figure 1 is a domain map (WW1, WW2, NLS, SDR) listing binding partners by domain; HIF-1alpha is listed with the first WW domain group and Tau, GSK-3beta and DVL2 with the SDR domain; no data.
entries.snippet: [figure attestation - pixels cannot be quote-matched] Figure 1: WWOX domain cartoon with two WW domains, NLS and SDR; boxes of PPXY-motif partners (p73, AP2g, ErbB-4, ezrin, SIMPLE, DVL1, DVL2, cJun, RUNX2), LPXY partner ITCH, WW1 partners (p53, DeltaNp63a, JNK1, Hyal-2, HIF-1a) and SDR partners (Tau, GSK-3b, DVL2).
